newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INTERVIEW-ABN Australia bank bid unlikely.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-ABN Australia bank bid unlikely.

text.p: The international head of ABN AMRO Bank said on Wednesday he would meet later this week with the architect of Australia's bank deregulation report who supported takeovers by multinationals such as the Dutch giant.
Michael Drabbe said, however, that his meeting with Stan Wallis in Melbourne this Friday was merely to hear the Australian businessman's views about the local industry.
ABN AMRO had run numbers on Australia's big four banks, Drabbe said, but was not likely to launch a takeover which would cost at least A$12 billion and up to A$26 billion.
"Acquisitions for us are one line of business. We have done our homework on virtually every bank in the areas of the world that are of interest to us," Drabbe said in an interview.

The Dutch bank has been cited by local brokers as one of about seven foreigners which could make a local bid in the not-too-distant future, even though they would be paying top dollar as the stocks carry a steep takeover premium.

"We are not ruling out Australia but we are already quite big in Australia. We don't want to get into head-on competition with the Australian market which is extremely well developed and very sophisticated in the consumer banking market."

Drabbe said acquisitions remained a key strategy of ABN AMRO but its sights were set elsewhere in Asia, Eastern Europe, Latin America, and the United States where it was already ranked as one of the 10 biggest outfits.

The bank had little option but to remain on the takeover trail in the United States because to hang back would cost market share, especially in Chicago and the Midwest region where it was based. ABN AMRO is the world's 14th largest bank with assets of more than US$400 billion of which more than US$87 billion are in North America.
Shareholders in Michigan-based Standard Federal Bancorp approved the US$1.9 billion takeover by ABN AMRO earlier this month.

"There are certain markets where acquisitions create a major leap forward. In the U.S., in the Midwest, we have little option. The Midwest for us is the second home market," said Drabbe, who added that the U.S. would account for about 25 percent of net profit in calendar 1997. The U.S. contribution in 1996 was 20 percent.
The bank was prepared to spend more than it paid for StanFed in the next round of acquisitions.
"We are looking selectively in Latin America, we are looking selectively in Europe," he said, ruling out expensive Western European operations and focussing instead on Eastern Europe.
"I think you probably won't see us make major acquisitions in Australia. In Asia, however, if that possibility would present itself we would be very interested".
Drabbe said the growth of overseas operations meant that ABN AMRO might have half of its profits derived from outside the Netherlands in calendar 1997. The figure at the end of 1996 was 44 percent.
"The target is 50 percent. We might well make that this year."

The Australian government released the Wallis Inquiry's report into the domestic financial system ealrier this month. It accepted the report's call for an end to the blanket-ban on foreign takeovers of the nation's four largest banks.
The four banks, all with assets of more than A$100 billion, are National Australia Bank Ltd, Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd, Commonweath Bank of Australia and Westpac Banking Corp.

The latter three have a market capitalisation of between A$12 billion and A$13 billion while NAB is valued at A$26.74 billion and is thought by most analysts to be a likely predator rather than an eventual prey.
